title: Manotoc v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court laid down strict requirements for the validity of substituted service of summons, ruling that the sheriff must show impossibility of personal service and the substituted service must comply with statutory requirements to satisfy due process.
doctrine: Substituted service of summons is extraordinary in character and may be used only as prescribed and in the circumstances authorized by statute. The impossibility of personal service must be shown by stating the efforts made to find the defendant and the fact that such efforts were unsuccessful.
fullText:
SANDOVAL-GUTIERREZ, J.:

The question before the Court is the validity of the substituted service of summons effected upon the petitioner.

Section 6 of Rule 14 of the Rules of Court provides that service of summons shall be made by handing a copy thereof to the defendant in person, or, if he refuses to receive and sign for it, by tendering it to him. It is only when the defendant cannot be served personally within a reasonable time that substituted service may be made.

The sheriff's return must show that the defendant could not be served within a reasonable time, the efforts made to locate the defendant, and the person to whom the summons was served. Substituted service must strictly comply with these requirements as it is in derogation of the usual method of service.
